blocks.text: a busy Saturday. While this was all well and good, it came with many downsides.
From sore calves and an aching lower back to a generally exhausted body at the end of the night, I was not in an overly happy place, especially when I got back home.
I loved the job but wished there was something I could do to limit these effects.
## Let’s Walk it Off For a long time, I couldn’t find the right balance.
After work, I would always be on my feet and once I got home, I found it so difficult to get moving.
No matter how many times I would tell myself to do some walking, I would always put it off until the next day.
## The Solution It was at the time I was looking into the possibility of a career change that I decided something had to give.
I couldn’t continue in my hospitality career because I would eventually end up burnt out, and I really loved my job.
I also needed to make changes for my health.
I wanted to get active and get that endorphin rush at the end of the day.
What I decided was that I was going to go to the gym after work (this is where I had to fake it) and that I would continue to put 30,000 steps on my Fitbit every day.
In doing so, I went from an average weight of 100kg to a weight of 80kg.
It was fantastic. Now that I’ve taken you back to my early twenties, I thought I would share a recent change I’ve made.
## The Current State Now I work from home.
A few years ago, I made a career change from the hospitality industry to the tech industry.

blocks.text: time was spent figuring out what we liked, what we didn’t, and what we wanted for our futures.
High school is the first time we get to choose our own path, and it also sets the foundation for the future.
High school allows us to see what is out there, and pick a “major” to move onto.
I’m assuming most readers here haven’t finished their undergrad yet, or are already graduated, and may have already moved on to a PhD, Master’s, or even a career.
But I’d like to talk about what is currently going on in my life: I am a PhD student.
First, let me tell you a bit about me.
I grew up in a small town in the province of Newfoundland, and Canada.
From early childhood until age 18, I wasn’t involved in many hobbies.
As a child, I did my fair share of piano, but never really practiced or progressed.
I played a little bit of soccer, which lasted for about a week before it was discontinued by my parents.
But at the age of 16 I picked up a new hobby that has lasted me for 5-6 years now: programming.
I was the average child. Went to school, came home, played some games, and did my homework.
But I was also a nerd. I loved programming, and in high school I got involved in all the after-school coding clubs that my school offered.
I would spend 2-3 hours at school in the evenings.
Then after school I was home on the computer for another 2-3 hours working on my own projects.
But I didn’t really know what I was doing.
Sure, I could write a program to create a list of primes, but could I write one to play a game?
That’s when I decided to focus my efforts more on programming.
At the time I was only involved in math, so I wanted to get my feet into physics a bit.

blocks.text: you are. ### Embracing Failure You can spend the rest of your life avoiding situations where failure is possible.
But it’ll still happen. The reality is that there are so many unknowns.
There’s only so much you can plan for.
The moment things go awry, your only option is to be proactive.
React and do what you can to overcome the situation at hand.
I like to consider myself to be a proactive person.
Most would probably disagree. There have been moments where I would be in my comfort zone.
All is well. The world isn’t coming to a stop.
Everything feels predictable, and I could take things for granted.
But all it takes is a single moment to throw me into reactive mode.
That one moment can snowball into something much bigger than I bargained for.
The worst part is that the only way out is through.
The next time you’re about to react to something, instead of succumbing to the situation, ask yourself.
What is a proactive way to handle this?
Sometimes the answer can be painful.
But every time you’re faced with an unfamiliar situation, you learn.
The next time, it’ll be easier.
### Staying in Control In some ways, the internet can be a terrible place.
There are too many trolls who’d do anything to get a reaction out of you.
One such instance was recently in the comments of one of my recent posts.
Someone was attacking my character and suggesting that I would never be able to become as successful as him.
I knew I could’ve let the comments go.
But instead, I replied. As expected, the trolls weren’t happy.
They kept on attacking. But I stayed true to myself.
It’s not their place to insult me or question my motivation to succeed.
People may try and discourage you.
It’s normal, and it’s something that we all have to endure.
But that doesn’t mean that you have to react.

blocks.text: this blog, I had an idea for a topic I might write about in my second post.
It was going to be about pragmatic empiricism and how it had shaped my thought.

I’m glad that this project took longer to get started than I anticipated, because when I went to find all the articles that I’d collected to make that post, a lot of them had been removed from the Web, and my copy of the paper copy of the paper didn’t have anything about pragmatism that I could remember.
I’ve still got a couple of books on pragmatism kicking around, though, and I’ve thought about those ideas a lot.
In many ways, that seems to have shaped my understanding of what science is.
It’s also shaped a lot of how I think about education, and the way that education can change the way that people understand the world around them.
Since a lot of what I write about on this blog has to do with science and education, it doesn’t seem like a bad place to mention pragmatism.
## Pragmatism The idea behind pragmatic empiricism is that knowledge consists of what has proven to be useful.
This means that it is an empirical question whether some proposed theory is actually true.

Of course, a lot of what passes for knowledge in our day and age really just consists of statements with no relation to reality, and even in science there are claims that seem, for no particular reason, to get repeated and repeated again, but it does at least try to keep things in check.
To be honest, I’ve only read a bit about pragmatism, and even what I’ve read was more or less a set of summaries by people with stronger training in this particular philosophy.

As a result, I can’t really say that I have any great insight into it, and I have to admit that I only have a kind of loose idea about what the authors of this particular school of thought might actually want me to say.

blocks.text: ever learned. In the years I have traveled through life, I’ve been given some pretty sweet gifts: my mom and dad.
I’m thankful for them in particular because I’ve gotten so much from them.
Not just from learning their names, not just from getting to know them as individuals, but also their relationship as people is very inspiring to me.
So much so, that I feel that I can learn some things from them without even knowing where they get their confidence from, how they treat others, etc.
I’ve never had to guess what love is, because they’ve always been there for me.
Not sure what a true definition would look like, but a love story that would be hard to top; it would be this.
They care about each other, and love the way each other is as individuals.
They also are best friends, which has been the coolest thing ever to witness in my life.
I’ve been blessed to have a childhood where I’ve never questioned who they truly are, because I’ve been allowed to live mine.
There hasn’t been any time where I can recall feeling like I needed something from them.
It wasn’t like there’s been a period where I’ve been missing something, a piece of who I am.
I think that’s why I’m happy, because the things I’ve been given are pretty special.
Not to mention, they are amazing people individually.
They’re a real joy to be around, and are always doing things that leave their stamp on the world.
They make time for their family, friends, and coworkers, which I think has a lot to do with how we’ve learned to love each other.
END NOTE Learning how to love each other is part of who we are as human beings.
The more we learn to trust each other, the better, I think.

Each day, I would check my word count: 10,000 so far?
Done! 20,000? Done. I was working toward 60,000 words, to keep me on track.
On vacation. With a deadline. But of course, I’m human.
The manuscript was finished on time, but it wasn’t exactly great.
Even when it was finished, I realized I’d left out huge chunks of content and needed to do more research for the ending and the middle.
I even took a break to write a new series of blog posts, instead of continuing to work on the manuscript.
I was determined to send in the full manuscript by the end of the deadline.
And in fact, I did. But I also knew in my heart that the manuscript wasn’t going to get me anywhere.

I didn’t finish my outline, so I had no idea what I was writing about.
I didn’t finish my outline, so I didn’t know where the characters would be going and how the story would progress.
I had a general sense of what was going to happen, and I knew what the problem was and what the ending would look like.
But the middle? It was very vague, and I didn’t finish fleshing it out until I was three-quarters of the way done.
The manuscript ended up being a huge mess.
I had to take breaks to fix it, but I was determined to continue.
This was going to be the book, even if it was a huge mess.
I knew it had the potential to be something, but I didn’t know how to make it better, so I just had to keep plowing through.
I had no idea what I was writing about.

blocks.text: , like an anchor in a storm. I hope they do the same for you.
If they don’t work for you, that’s fine.
That’s okay. You’re not a Buddhist.
But if they do, I hope you’ll keep them in mind as we’re collectively facing an unprecedented disaster.
So often, crises like these turn us against each other.
They’re not about love, and they’re definitely not about justice.
The world can seem a lonely place at these times, a bleak landscape where people are only out for themselves.
Where all we have is ourselves.
It’s a time when we can really use Buddha, dharma, sangha, justice.
Not just during our meditation, but also as the basis of our lives.
Buddha is the first refuge, and it’s as simple as that.
Whether you believe the historical Gautama Siddhartha existed or not, it doesn’t matter.
The historical Buddha means little.
What matters is this: You have the potential to wake up, and so do I.
We are the Buddhas of today. All the Buddhas of all the ages are only Buddhas because of me, because of you.
The dharma refuge is about mindfulness, a way to bring the body and mind into the present moment.
When mindfulness is present, you’re not lost in your own worries or other people’s pain.
You’re in the moment, in the presence of others.
That’s a refuge I can always count on.
I’ve been doing this a while now, but I’m not the sangha.
In my meditation groups, I share with people who’ve been meditating for a long time, since the days when the only way to do meditation was to sit with the Buddha under a tree.
So what does the refuge of sangha mean to me?
It means that they’re there for me, to share this journey.
And I’ll do the same for them.
The last refuge is about justice.
